band.text:
The library in the cottage is a shelf of field guides, the county avifauna, forty bound years of the log
and a box of reprints, and it is for use in the cottage rather than for borrowing. A volunteer who
wants a book at home asks the recorder, who will usually say yes and write it in the loans book, and
will usually remember. The bound logs never leave the building, because they are the only copy and
the observatory has no fire safe.

The tea is free to volunteers and a pound to visitors, the biscuits are whatever the last person
brought, and the kettle is the only appliance in the cottage that is never switched off at the wall. The
mugs are washed by whoever drinks from them. This is written down because it was once not, and
the resulting week was long.

The observatory closes for the first two weeks of January, when the cottage is cleaned, the hides are
repaired, the store is emptied and dried, and the log is bound and shelved. The census is walked
even then, by the warden, because forty years without a gap is a thing worth keeping.

provenance.key:
where anglers are not allowed. The report goes to the trust by telephone the same day and is
written in the log.

Winter storms are the observatory's weather, and the cottage has a storm routine on a card by the
door: shutters, the balcony telescope indoors, the ringing store door braced, the boardwalk closed
with the chain, and the far hide checked after the storm by two people together in daylight. A storm
surge in 2013 put a foot of water through the store and the routine was written the following week.

The migration seasons, late April and September into October, bring the most birds, the most
visitors and the most volunteers, and the rota for those weeks is drawn up in the month before and
pinned on the cottage wall. Anyone who can offer a full week in either season is asked to, because
the census is worth more walked by the same eyes for seven days than by seven different pairs.

Rarities are reported to the county recorder by the warden, not by the finder, and are not put on the
internet until the recorder has agreed and the trust has said whether the marsh can take the
visitors. A rare bird in the far section in winter is a rare bird nobody is told about until it has gone,
because the spit will not carry a crowd and the tide will not wait for one.

Photographers are welcome and are asked for the same things as everyone else: the boardwalk,
quiet in the hides, and no playback of calls anywhere on the reserve. A photograph taken from the
balcony is the observatory's to use in the report and the guidebook if the photographer agrees, and
most do, with a credit.

The annual report is written in January by the warden and the recorder, is short, and gives the
census totals by species and month, the ringing totals and recoveries, the visitor numbers, what
went wrong and what is planned. It is read at the March meeting and sent to the trust, the county
and the universities, and a copy goes on the shelf beside the forty before it.

Complaints are few and are about dogs, parking or a volunteer who was short with somebody on a
difficult day. They go to the chair, are answered within the week, and are written in the log with the
answer. A volunteer who was short with somebody is asked about it, once, and the matter is then
closed.

New volunteers do three shifts alongside somebody who has been coming for years before they
take a desk or a hide alone, and they walk the census with the warden at least twice before they
walk it by themselves. After that they are on the list and are asked what they would like to learn;
most say ringing, and most are told it takes two seasons.
